# Proposition 39 (California General Election, November 3, 2026)

**Full title:** "PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT."

**Ballot origin:** Placed on the ballot by petition signatures.

**Summary:** The measure would invalidate mail ballots that lack the last four digits of a designated government-issued identification number written on the envelope. It would also prohibit in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification.

**Fiscal impact:** Implementing the new voting requirements would cost tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year.

**What a YES vote means:** Voters would have to provide additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.

**What a NO vote means:** Voter identity would continue to be established by signature.

## Arguments

**For (Yes):**
- Presents a bipartisan voter ID solution, which the campaign says is supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters.
- Argues it would increase trust and confidence in elections.

**Against (No):**
- Argues the measure would add costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible voters.
- Warns it could expose personal information to identity theft.
- Says it would waste hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars.
- Links the measure to a political agenda, claiming it advances "Trump's voter suppression agenda."

## Supporters and Opponents

- **Supporters:** The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women's Leadership Assn
- **Opponents:** ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California

## Campaign Contacts

- **Yes:** Californians for Voter ID, Info@voteridca.org, www.VoterIDCA.org
- **No:** Californians for Voting Rights, info@caforvotingrights.org, CAforvotingrights.org (note: this link on the page actually points to noonprop39.com)

## Key Dates

- **October 5, 2026:** Counties begin mailing ballots on or before this date.
- **October 19, 2026:** Last day to register to vote.
- **November 3, 2026:** Election Day. Polls are open 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.

input.prompt: Provide the full Legislative Analyst's analysis of this proposition in detail: background on current law, what the proposal would do (all provisions — in-person ID requirements, mail ballot requirements, which IDs count, free ID provisions, voter roll citizenship verification, audits, etc.), fiscal effects, and any other details.

Provide the full text (or a very detailed summary) of the argument in favor, rebuttal to the argument in favor, argument against, and rebuttal to the argument against. Include who signed each argument.

content.content:
**Background (Current Law)**

- **Administration:** Counties run most elections, including printing and mailing ballots. The Secretary of State oversees statewide elections and prepares the state Voter Information Guide.
- **Citizenship:** Only U.S. citizens may vote in state and federal elections and in nearly all local elections. San Francisco and Oakland allow certain noncitizen parents, guardians, or caregivers to vote only in school board elections.
- **Registration:** Applicants must be U.S. citizens, California residents, at least 18, not in prison, and not ruled unable to vote by a court. Falsely claiming citizenship is perjury. People can register online, by mail, in person, or through the DMV. Identity is established with a driver's license number, state ID number, or last four digits of a Social Security number. Those who don't provide these may be asked for ID the first time they vote.
- **Roll maintenance:** Officials must remove ineligible voters, using updates from other agencies about deaths and imprisonment.
- **Voting:** All registered voters receive a vote-by-mail ballot. In the November 2024 election, about 16 million Californians voted, about 13 million by mail and about 3 million in person.
- **Identification now:** In-person voters sign a roster. Mail voters sign the ballot envelope, and those signatures are verified. In-person signatures generally are not.
- **State Auditor:** This independent, nonpartisan office reviews government performance and can recommend improvements.

**Proposal (Proposition 39)**

1. **Citizenship verification:** State and local officials must make "best efforts" to use government data to verify that registered voters are citizens. Each year, they must report the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship has been verified.
2. **Mail-voting ID selection:** New and existing voters must choose a government-issued ID on their registration in order to vote by mail.
3. **ID at every election:** Voters must provide additional identifying information in every California election:
   - **In person:** Show a government-issued ID.
   - **By mail:** Write the last four digits of the selected ID number on the ballot envelope. Officials must match these to registration records.
   - Officials must verify identity before counting any ballot.
4. **Free state voter ID card:** The state must provide a voter ID card at no cost to anyone who requests one. The card could serve as the government-issued ID for voting.
5. **Audits:** In every odd-numbered year, the State Auditor must report on how well the state and each county comply and recommend improvements.
6. **Further legislation:** The Legislature must pass additional laws to implement the measure. The measure leaves key details undefined, including which IDs are acceptable and what counts as "best efforts" for verifying citizenship.

**Fiscal Effects**

- **Costs:** State and local costs would rise by tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year. That is less than 0.25 percent of the state's General Fund budget.
- **Cost drivers:** Actual costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. Examples include the design of the ID card and how many cards are requested.
- **Possible savings:** Savings could come from fewer registered voters, such as through removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters who lack government-issued ID. The LAO expects these savings likely would not exceed the costs.

**Other Details**

The analysis points to official sites listing committees formed to support or oppose the measure and their top contributors.

**Argument in Favor of Prop. 39**
*Signed by Margit Whitlock (Democratic Coalition Chair), Tafa Jefferson (Republican Coalition Chair), and Joe Green (Independent Coalition Chair), Californians for Voter ID*

- Presents voter ID as a bipartisan way to build trust and participation, noting that nearly half the measure's signatures came from Democratic and Independent voters.
- Says the measure keeps mail ballots and extended polling hours, accepts a range of government IDs, and guarantees a free voter ID for anyone who wants one.
- Criticizes the current signature-matching process as slow and says more than 100,000 ballots were rejected in the last election over signature mismatches.
- Argues that voter ID increases turnout, citing states with ID laws and free IDs for eligible voters.
- Says the measure requires officials to keep voter lists accurate, check that only citizens are registered, and conduct an independent audit every two years.
- Lists supporters including the Latino American Political Association, California Women's Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, and the Transparency Foundation.

**Rebuttal to Argument in Favor**
*Signed by Alex Padilla (U.S. Senator for California), Catherine Kennedy (President, California Nurses Association), and Adam Weinberger (President, California School Employees Association)*

- Calls the measure voter suppression that makes voting harder and more expensive, and says it is funded by MAGA-aligned billionaires.
- Says California election officials already verify voters, so the measure only adds hurdles.
- Claims Texas threw out 12 times more mail ballots than California when it tried a similar approach.
- Says the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office found the measure could cost hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
- Argues the measure creates identity theft risks and distracts from issues like hospital closures, wildfire recovery, and cost of living.

**Argument Against Prop. 39**
*Signed by David Trujillo (Executive Director, ACLU California Action), Darius Kemp (California State Director, Common Cause), and Lorrel Plimier (Co-President, League of Women Voters of California)*

- Frames opposition around what it describes as Donald Trump's false claims about elections and his efforts to gain power, citing other actions it opposes.
- Says the measure wastes hundreds of millions of dollars on election conspiracy theories.
- Warns that mail voters would have to put personal details on return envelopes, creating identity theft risks.
- Says a personal ID number must exactly match state records, so a single error could void a valid ballot, and outdated addresses or name misspellings could lead to rejection. Voters who don't opt in may not receive a mail ballot.
- Argues that "free" IDs still carry costs like transportation, time off work, childcare, and required documents, which would hit seniors, students, low-income workers, voters of color, and women who changed their names.

**Rebuttal to Argument Against**
*Signed by Johnathan Hale (Executive Director, The Transparency Foundation), Cynthia Kaui (Executive Director, California Women's Leadership Association), and Ed Cervantes (President, Latino American Political Association)*

- Says the measure is bipartisan and not about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom, but a California response to declining trust in elections.
- Says it improves voter list accuracy and requires independent audits.
- Argues that states with voter ID laws have not seen declines in participation.
- Says supporters span parties, ages, genders, and communities, and that the measure keeps voting accessible for eligible voters.

Here's what the search turned up on California's Prop 39 (voter ID), mostly from CalMatters:

**What it would do**
- Proposition 39, also known as the California voter ID initiative, is an initiated constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026 ballot. That's today, and no results showed up in the search.
- In a CalMatters op-ed, Bill Jones, a former state elections chief, says it requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It also directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, and it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship.
- Under current law, California requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places.
- SPUR points out that the proposition language does not specify which forms of ID would qualify or how citizenship would be verified. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.

**Who's behind it and who's paying**
- CalMatters says it was placed on the ballot by conservative groups. Assemblymember Carl DeMaio announced that supporters will submit more than 1.3 million signatures to qualify the measure for the November 2026 ballot, at a press conference on March 3, 2026.
- A CalMatters story from October reports that Illinois businessman Richard Uhilein and venture capitalists Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss are among the big spenders bankrolling California's voter ID measure. (CalMatters' spelling; the name is usually Uihlein.) Republican megadonors hope its success, or failure, can reveal how similar measures can perform in more moderate states.

**Arguments**
- Supporters: ID requirements at voting sites will strengthen voters' trust in California's election process, and most states require voters to show some form of identification to vote.
- Opponents: requiring ID will make it harder for eligible voters who don't have a driver's license or other supporting documents to vote. The CalMatters opposing op-ed also argues that instituting more stringent voter identification processes would have major fiscal impacts to California taxpayers.

**Polling and context**
- Wikipedia lists these polls: PPIC, May 14–18, 2026: 49% / 51%; Berkeley IGS, April 9–18: 56% / 39% / 6%; Berkeley IGS, March 9–15: 44% / 45% / 12%. The column headers weren't in the results, but the order is probably yes / no / undecided.
- Californians will vote on 14 ballot propositions in the November 2026 election. Nevada, North Carolina, and Oklahoma will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots.

**SPUR's analysis of Prop 39 (California Voter ID)**

**Background**
- The federal Voting Rights Act of 1965 once gave federal oversight of elections in jurisdictions with histories of discrimination, but recent Supreme Court decisions have weakened key parts. SPUR says this gives states more room to adopt stricter voter ID laws.
- Under the 2002 Help America Vote Act, first-time federal voters who registered by mail must show ID. California also verifies registrants with a driver's license number, state ID number, or last four Social Security digits, and states check signatures on mail ballots.
- Of the 36 states that require some ID at the polls, nine have "strict" laws requiring photo or other ID to cast a regular ballot. The rest allow voters without ID to sign an affidavit.
- In September 2024, California enacted SB 1174, which bars local governments from setting their own voter ID requirements. In January 2026, the California Supreme Court struck down Huntington Beach's local voter ID measure. A 2025 state bill (AB 25) on statewide voter ID failed in committee on a party-line vote. A federal bill, the SAVE America Act (H.R. 7296), has also been introduced.
- Prop 39 was pursued by Reform California, the organization of Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, through the signature-gathering process. It needs a simple majority to pass.

**What It Would Do**
- Require voters to show government-issued ID at the polls, or provide the last four digits of a government ID number when voting by mail.
- Require the state to give a free voter ID card to any voter who asks for one.
- Require the Secretary of State and county election officials to verify citizenship attestations and report yearly the share of each county's voter rolls that have been verified.
- The measure does not define which IDs qualify or how citizenship would be verified. It leaves those details to future legislation.

**Pros**
- SPUR could not identify any benefits.

**Cons**
- Studies find voter ID laws do not reduce actual or perceived voter fraud.
- ID requirements can block eligible voters, increase ballot rejections from data-entry errors, slow voting, and burden people who struggle to take time off work, travel to government offices, or gather documents.
- Printing partial ID numbers on mail-ballot envelopes, alongside names and addresses, could raise identity-theft risks when combined with data from other breaches.
- Costs to state and local governments would be substantial: an estimated tens of millions of dollars in one-time costs, and ongoing annual costs of tens to hundreds of millions, depending on future legislation.
- Equity: voters of color, low-income people, older adults, students, people with disabilities, and those who have changed their names are less likely to have the required IDs. SPUR cites an ACLU estimate that about 13% of Black Americans lack acceptable voter ID, compared with 5% of white Americans.

**SPUR's Recommendation: Vote NO**
- California already has election integrity safeguards. Voters certify eligibility under penalty of perjury, in-person voters sign the roster, mail ballots undergo signature verification, and illegal voting is a felony.
- SPUR says California has no evidence of widespread voter fraud, and research links strict ID requirements to barriers for voters who lack acceptable ID.
- SB 1174 already restricts local voter ID rules, and Prop 39 would override that.
- SPUR argues that the high implementation costs, on already strained budgets, aren't justified without evidence of significant fraud.

# Summary: Proposition 39 (Voter ID), per the California Budget & Policy Center

The source is a September 2026 issue brief from the California Budget & Policy Center, which opposes the measure. It is a critical analysis, not a neutral one, and it summarizes proponents' arguments only briefly.

## What Prop. 39 Would Do

- **Citizenship verification:** Requires state and county officials to "use best efforts" to verify registered voters' citizenship using "government data." Neither term is defined, and counties would annually report the share of voters verified.
- **In-person voting:** Voters would show a "government-issued" ID at the polls. The measure does not define that term, so the Legislature would have to.
- **Mail voting:** All new and existing voters would choose a government-issued ID that goes into their registration record. Voters would write the last four digits of that ID's number on the outside of the ballot envelope, and officials would check them against the registration record.
- **New state voter ID card:** The state would issue a free voter ID card to eligible voters who request one.
- **Audits:** The State Auditor would audit state and county compliance in odd-numbered years.
- **Implementing law:** The Legislature would have to "promptly enact laws" to implement the measure, including rules for military and overseas voters.
- **Private lawsuits:** Any citizen could sue the state or a county for alleged noncompliance.

## Costs

- The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates **annual state and local costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars**. The brief cites this as its main fiscal source.
- The measure has no new revenue, so costs would come from existing budgets at a time when H.R. 1 is also raising county costs, by an estimated $6 billion to $9.5 billion a year.
- The LAO suggests possible "savings" if fewer people register, but says any savings "likely would not exceed the costs of the measure."
- Cost drivers include the State Auditor's expanded staff, Secretary of State and county staffing, IT systems for citizenship checks, and the voter ID card.

## Who Would Be Affected

- **People without current licenses:** About 2.7 million voting-age citizens (10.8%) have no driver's license. Another 3 million-plus (12.6%) have an expired, out-of-state, or outdated license.
- **Groups less likely to have a license:** People of color, young people, people with lower incomes or less education, and people with disabilities.
- **Young Californians:** Ages 18–34 are about 30% of adults but 21% of likely voters (PPIC). The brief says they move more often, cast more provisional ballots, and are less likely to have licenses.
- **Communities of color:** A Texas study cited in the brief found that registrants voting without ID were disproportionately Black and Latinx.
- **Mail voters:** Mail voting is the most common method in California, so identity-theft concerns could deter these voters.

## ID Ownership Data (VoteRiders/CDCE survey)

- 24% of citizens without a driver's license also lack a state ID card.
- Only 29% of that group have a current, readily accessible passport.
- Only 13% have a current public school ID.
- 6 in 10 voting-age citizens expressed confusion about current in-person ID rules.
- Many cited cost and wait time for obtaining an ID.

## Mail Ballot Risks

The brief does not give rejection-rate data. Its concerns are these:

- **Identity theft:** Partial ID numbers on envelopes would add to the name, address, and signature already there. Envelopes are stored for six to 22 months.
- **Privacy standards:** The brief cites NIST guidance that partial identifiers are still considered personally identifiable information.
- **Deterrence:** Fear of identity theft could push some voters away from mail voting.
- **Matching failures:** Ballots would have to match the digits on file to be counted. The brief implies mismatches would cause problems but does not quantify them.

## Evidence Cited

**Fraud is rare:**
- A Brookings analysis using a Heritage Foundation fraud database found roughly 3 to 15 fraudulent votes out of 10 million in seven close-outcome states.
- The Brennan Center concludes voter impersonation is extremely rare.
- A 2016 national survey found about 30 suspected noncitizen voting referrals, about 0.0001% of votes cast.
- The Bipartisan Policy Institute and Cato Institute both find no good evidence noncitizen voting has changed an outcome.

**Confidence and ID laws:**
- A Stanford Law Review study found similar voter confidence in strict-ID and minimum-ID states.
- Research by UC Riverside and Western Washington University found strict ID laws had little to no effect on confidence, which the authors attribute to partisanship.

**Citizenship databases:**
- Federal databases have "errors, inconsistencies, and outdated information," according to the Brennan Center.
- Name changes and naturalized citizens' records can produce false mismatches.
- A Missouri election official is quoted expressing doubt about the accuracy of the SAVE database.

**Other context:**
- Other states have recently passed stricter voter ID laws, and six states have measures on the fall ballot.
- Researchers cited in the brief describe the cost of voting in general as a barrier, particularly for young people.

## Proponents and Opponents

- **Supporters:** Led by Assemblymember Carl DeMaio. Also the California Republican Party, Reform California, and Richard Uihlein.
- **Opponents:** Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, Sen. Alex Padilla, the ACLU, Common Cause, the League of Women Voters, and the California Democratic Party.

- **Rate:** The Secretary of State's official count was 24,363 mail-in ballots rejected, a rejection rate of 12.4 percent. 12.87% of Democratic mail-in ballots were rejected, compared with 11.77% of Republican ballots. In addition, 12,000 absentee ballot applications were rejected.

**Author:** Bill Jones, a former California secretary of state who served two terms as the state's chief elections officer. The piece is a guest commentary published by CalMatters.

**Argument:** Jones supports Proposition 39, the November 2026 ballot measure requiring voter ID. He argues that election integrity and voter participation support each other. He writes that "A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages," so public confidence in the count is essential. He says Prop. 39 is a modest reform that makes California's elections harder to doubt, and he rejects the idea that it is partisan.

**Measure's provisions (as he describes them):**
- In-person voters must show government-issued ID, and mail voters must provide the last four digits of a government ID number.
- The state must issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so he argues it creates no poll tax.
- Election officials must keep voter rolls accurate, including verifying citizenship.

**Evidence and supporting points:**
- **Other states:** About 36 states already require some form of voter ID, according to the NCSL.
- **Voter rolls:** He says California's voter file has not been reliably cleaned of duplicates, deceased voters, and people who should not have been added.
- **Mail voting and ballot harvesting:** He notes that the state automatically mails ballots to people who have moved and allows ballot harvesting, which did not exist when he ran elections.
- **Mexico anecdote:** He recalls observing late-1990s Mexican elections, where voter ID and inked fingers helped rebuild public trust. He concedes security measures alone did not explain the political change there.
- **Ballot title dispute:** The measure qualified with bipartisan signature support. He criticizes the Attorney General's July revision of the ballot title, which he says now suggests the measure "prohibits" citizens from voting without ID.

**Limits of the argument:** He acknowledges that "None of that means fraud is rampant." His case rests on reducing the system's checks and strengthening public confidence, not on documented widespread fraud. The article also notes that an opposing commentary, which warns of unnecessary barriers, is available separately.

**Author:** Marisol Ramirez, a member of the Inland Empire Latino Giving Circle who has worked for nearly two decades on civic participation. CalMatters published the piece as a guest commentary in its California Voices forum in August 2026.

**Core argument:** Ramirez opposes Proposition 39, which would require a government-issued ID for in-person voting and the last four digits of a government ID on mail-in ballots. She argues that:

- Her core principle is that "democracy is strongest when elections are both accessible and secure."
- California already verifies voter eligibility. Registrants attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury and provide identity information, so Prop. 39 is redundant and adds barriers.
- Eligible voters could be wrongly denied the ballot, especially Latinos and young people.
- Immigrant and mixed-status communities already hesitate to share personal information with government, and a new ID requirement could deepen that hesitation.
- Fraud is extremely rare, so the measure addresses a problem that barely exists.
- Creating a new ID form would carry significant costs for a state facing budget deficits, even if the ID itself is free.

**Evidence cited:**

- **University of Maryland survey (linked via a UMD center report):** Over 1 in 4 Latino adults lack a driver's license showing their current name or address, and 41% of 18–24-year-olds are in a similar situation.
- **Brennan Center for Justice:** Voter fraud incidents range from 0.0003% to 0.0025%.
- **Legislative Analyst's Office:** Estimated the cost of creating the new ID at tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars.
- **California Secretary of State:** Cited for the citizenship attestation requirement in voter registration and for the figure of more than 27 million eligible voters.
- **Other sources:** A CalMatters article on DMV data sharing with immigrants, and a Forum Together article on noncitizen voting, which the op-ed cites for the point that noncitizen voting is a federal crime.

# Hoover Institution's Analysis of Proposition 39 (California Voter ID Initiative)

## What It Does
Proposition 39 is an initiated constitutional amendment with three main parts:
- **In-person voting:** Voters must show government-issued ID.
- **Mail-in voting:** Voters must write the last four digits of a government ID number on the ballot envelope. That number is matched against their registration record.
- **Supporting provisions:** The state must provide a free voter ID card on request, maintain accurate voter rolls, verify citizenship using government data, and report the verified share each year. The State Auditor must publish a compliance audit every odd-numbered year, and any citizen can seek judicial review.

Hoover notes that more than two-thirds of states already require ID to receive a ballot, and that California is among the few that asks for none at the polls.

## Evidence on Effects

**Turnout and access:** Hoover does not present direct evidence on turnout effects. It argues that the state's existing "cure" process, which lets officials contact voters and allows 22 days after Election Day to fix ballot problems, should limit the risk that valid votes are rejected. It also acknowledges that ID rules can cause honest mistakes that reject eligible ballots.

**Fraud:** Hoover says there is "no credible proof of widespread or systematic election fraud in California." It notes that in-person impersonation is the rarest documented fraud type. Its main concern is mail-in voting, which it says lacks a rigorous way to confirm who actually filled out the ballot. It also points to ballot harvesting, since harvesters' required name and signature cannot be verified. Hoover adds that fraud statistics only capture detected fraud.

**Confidence:** Hoover reports declining confidence in whether national elections are counted correctly and in general election honesty. It also notes a "winner-loser effect," where confidence rises or falls with whether a voter's preferred candidate won. It links the shift toward mail voting to some of this anxiety but does not claim a proven causal link.

## Costs
The page does not discuss fiscal costs of implementation. It refers readers to the LAO ballot analysis for that information.

## Legal Issues
- **Ballot title:** The Attorney General changed the title to "Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification." Proponents challenged it as misleading. The Sacramento Superior Court ruled the title and summary "sufficient."
- **Constitutional status:** Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot simply repeal it. It must enact implementing laws.
- **Self-executing provisions:** The measure takes effect on passage, and it allows any citizen to seek judicial remedy for noncompliance.

## Strengths (as Hoover frames them)
- Aligns California with most other states and with broad bipartisan public support (over 75 percent in cited polls).
- Addresses a verification gap in mail-in voting.
- Free ID cards reduce barriers for people without a driver's license.
- Builds in regular audits and public reporting.

## Weaknesses and Trade-offs (as Hoover frames them)
- Some eligible ballots could be rejected for honest mistakes.
- Hoover describes a fundamental trade-off between election legitimacy and ease of voting.
- Its effect on fraud and confidence is uncertain, and it may not address the mail-in and ballot harvesting concerns it identifies.

## Conclusion
Hoover does not explicitly recommend a vote. It frames Proposition 39 as asking voters "whether increased legitimacy is worth making voting slightly more difficult." Its analysis leans toward the measure's merits, particularly its gap-closing purpose, while acknowledging that the cure process is needed to limit wrongful rejections.

# Proposition 39: Voter Identification (November 3, 2026)

**Background**
- Proposition 39 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment. It was filed with the Attorney General on July 16, 2025, and approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025.
- Proponents needed 874,641 valid signatures. They submitted about 1.37 million on March 2, 2026, and the measure qualified on April 24, 2026.
- On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID sued the Secretary of State over the revised ballot title, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta. The plaintiffs said the title omitted the original reference to additional ID and citizenship verification. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court ruled for the state, so the measure stays on the ballot with its title unchanged.

**What the measure would do**
- **Citizenship verification:** Election officials would make "best efforts," using government records, to verify registered voters' citizenship and report annually by county on the percentage verified.
- **Registration and mail voting:** Voters would select a government-issued ID form when registering to vote by mail. The state would provide a free voter ID card to anyone who requests one.
- **Voting:** In-person voters would show government-issued ID. Mail voters would write the last four digits of their ID number on the ballot envelope, and officials would check them against registration records.
- **Oversight:** The State Auditor would review state and county compliance in every odd-numbered year. The Legislature would need to fill in missing details and pass further laws before full implementation.

**Fiscal impact (Legislative Analyst's Office)**
- State and local costs would rise by an estimated tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year, depending on implementation.
- That is less than 0.25% of the General Fund budget.
- Major cost drivers include the ID card program, administrative requirements, and how many people request cards.
- Some savings could result if ineligible or unidentified voters are removed from the rolls.

**Arguments**
- **Supporters** say ID requirements would boost confidence in elections and add safeguards. They point to similar rules elsewhere and argue that universal mail ballots and ballot collection increase the need for identity checks. They do not claim widespread fraud is occurring.
- **Opponents** say the measure adds barriers for eligible voters without fixing a documented problem. They warn of wrongful ballot rejections, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities. They also raise privacy concerns about partial ID numbers on envelopes and cite high administrative costs.

I'm not going to give you a one-word yes or no on this one. Voter ID is one of the most partisan election fights in the country, and the right vote depends on how you weigh things people reasonably disagree about. Here's what my research found, so you can decide quickly.

**What Prop 39 does**
- It amends the state constitution, so changing it later would take another ballot measure.
- To vote in person, you'd show a government ID.
- To vote by mail, you'd write the last 4 digits of an ID number on the envelope. It must match your registration record, and it's checked in addition to your signature. Ballots without it don't count.
- The state would give a free voter ID card to anyone who asks.
- Officials would have to try to verify voters' citizenship using government records. The State Auditor would check how well the state and counties follow the rules every two years, and any citizen could sue if they don't.
- The Legislature would fill in key details later, including which IDs count.
- The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office estimates it would cost tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

**What the evidence shows**
- **Fraud is rare.** Even supporters, like former Republican Secretary of State Bill Jones and the Hoover Institution, don't claim it's widespread in California.
- **Turnout and trust:** The largest study of strict ID laws (Cantoni & Pons, 2021) found no measurable effect on turnout. It also found no effect on actual fraud or on how much fraud people believe happens. Other studies find little effect on voter confidence.
- **Mail ballots:** Requiring ID numbers on mail ballots has increased rejections elsewhere. In Texas, rejections went from 0.9% in 2020 to about 12% in its first election under the rule, then settled around 3.5%. California rejected 0.9% in 2024. California gives voters more time to fix ballot problems, but how that would work here is up to the Legislature.
- **Court rulings:** A judge tentatively found that the Yes campaign's claims that Prop 39 would make voting easier, protect privacy, and save money were false or misleading, and the campaign removed them. The Yes side also lost its challenge to the official ballot title, which it calls biased.

**You'd likely lean yes if** you see an ID check as a reasonable baseline (36 states require some form) and value building trust more than the cost. You'd also have to be comfortable putting it in the constitution with the details left for later.

**You'd likely lean no if** you put more weight on how rare fraud is, the cost, the risk of valid mail ballots being rejected, and the privacy concern about ID digits on envelopes. You might also object to locking undefined rules into the constitution.

**Who's on each side**
- **Yes:** California Republican Party, Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Orange County Register.
- **No:** California Democratic Party, Gov. Newsom, ACLU, League of Women Voters, and the San Francisco Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, San Diego Union-Tribune, and Mercury News editorial boards.

Sources:
- [CA Voter Guide: Prop 39](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/), [LAO analysis](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm), [Arguments and rebuttals](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)
- [CalMatters guide](https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), [Bill Jones op-ed (yes)](https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-identification-proposition-39-elections/)
- [Hoover Proposition Lab](https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-39), [SPUR](https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-39-california-voter-id), [CA Budget & Policy Center](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-39-explained-what-voter-id-would-mean-for-california/)
- [Cantoni & Pons study (NBER)](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25522)
- [Colorado Sun on other states' rejection rates](https://coloradosun.com/2026/10/21/amendment-84-other-states-ballot-rejections/), [CA 2024 ballot rejections](https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2025/03/20/california-elections-officials-rejected-122000-ballots-in-2024-election-heres-why/)
